description: We are a diverse team of students from Nile University and 6th of October University, passionate about technology, AI, software development, and space exploration. Our team brings experience in machine learning, cybersecurity, and software engineering, along with a strong interest in solving real-world challenges using NASA's open data. We're looking to collaborate with motivated participants who bring creativity, scientific knowledge, data analysis, or engineering skills.
summary: Nazeer (“counterpart” in Arabic) is a web app that finds the places on Earth that most resemble a chosen spot on the Moon or Mars. Users explore NASA Trek imagery of either body, click a map tile or enter coordinates, and instantly see the surface geology of that area and the top three Earth analogs, each with a confidence score and a NASA GIBS satellite preview. We built a pipeline that harmonizes three incompatible datasets (GLiM for Earth, USGS geologic maps for the Moon and Mars) onto a common grid and compares their rock-type composition. Where no trustworthy match exists, Nazeer says so instead of forcing one. This addresses the challenge by giving mission planners a familiar Earth reference for candidate base locations, so teams can pick training, testing, and prototyping sites before committing to expensive lunar or Martian analysis. It is a screening tool, not a landing-site assessment.
details:
What it does

Nazeer (“counterpart” in Arabic) is a web app that helps find places on Earth that resemble a chosen location on the Moon or Mars. You pick a body, then either click a tile on a NASA map or type a latitude and longitude. The app shows the surface geology of that spot and the three closest Earth analogs. Each one has a confidence score, the breakdown of rock types, and a NASA satellite preview of the matched area. If no trustworthy match exists, Nazeer says “No reliable analog” instead of forcing one.

How it works

We combined three geological datasets that were never designed to work together: GLiM for Earth, the USGS Unified Geologic Map of the Moon, and the USGS Geologic Map of Mars. Each uses its own classification system and map scale. We built a Python pipeline that overlays them on a common grid, calculates the area of every rock unit in each grid cell, and groups the units into simple classes such as volcanic, impact, plains, highlands, sedimentary, and ice. The Moon and Mars use a 10° grid. Earth uses a finer 5° grid built from the GLiM raster.

When a user selects a location, the backend compares the class mix of that area with every eligible Earth cell and ranks them. Classes with no Earth equivalent, such as impact craters, lower the confidence rather than being forced into a match. The results are spread out geographically so the three suggestions are different regions.

Benefits and impact

Earth analogs let engineers, scientists, and planners test equipment, train crews, and study processes in places they can actually reach. Nazeer gives them a quick, transparent starting point when looking at candidate base locations on the Moon and Mars. It is a screening tool, not a landing-site assessment, and the app states its limits clearly.

Tools

The frontend uses React, TypeScript, Vite, and Leaflet. The backend uses Python and FastAPI. Data processing was done in Python with GIS tools. We used NASA Trek for the Moon and Mars imagery and NASA GIBS for the Earth previews. The app has no database and needs no API keys, and it is deployed on Vercel.

What else we did

We also built a second pipeline that compares terrain shape (slope, relief, roughness) from NASA LOLA and MOLA elevation data. We validated it with GMT, Excel, and NASA Trek checks. We left it out of the final app because the data was too coarse to be reliable.
